title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
directAnswer: Find the longest window with all distinct characters. The interview-grade answer is a variable-size sliding window: expand the right edge, and when you hit a repeat, jump the left edge to just past the duplicate's last seen index. A hash map of char → last index makes the jump O(1). One pass, O(n) time, O(min(n, alphabet)) space.

rules: On a repeat, jump `left` to `last[c] + 1` — don't crawl it one step at a time.
Guard with `last[c] >= left`: a duplicate *outside* the current window must be ignored.
Update `last[c] = right` every iteration, even when no jump happens.
Window length is `right − left + 1`; take the max after each expansion.
Set-based variant works too but shrinks left in a loop; the index map jumps in O(1).
whenToUse: Longest/shortest contiguous window satisfying a 'no repeats' or distinctness constraint
You can extend the window on the right and only ever need to move left forward
A per-character last position lets you skip the left pointer ahead
Brute force enumerates all substrings and you want a single pass
antiSignals: Order doesn't matter / subsequences allowed → not a contiguous-window problem
Need at most k distinct (not zero repeats) → window with a count map (LC340)
Fixed window size → simpler fixed sliding window (Permutation in String)
remember.takeaway: A window that only ever grows on the right and jumps left forward on a violation is the variable sliding-window template. The 'remember each element's last index to jump the left edge' trick generalizes to many substring problems.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you use a variable sliding window with a last-seen-index map to achieve one pass, instead of re-checking every substring, and whether you correctly avoid moving the left edge backward.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Setting left = last[c] + 1 even when the duplicate is outside the window (moving left backward), or forgetting to update last[c] when no jump occurs.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the O(n³)/O(n²) brute force, then 'a window with a last-index map jumps left in O(1)'. Call out the `last[c] >= left` guard that prevents the left pointer from regressing.

problemStatement:
Given a string `s`, find the length of the **longest substring** without repeating characters.

A substring is a contiguous, non-empty sequence of characters within the string.
constraints: s consists of English letters, digits, symbols and spaces
understanding: We want the longest contiguous run in which no character repeats. 'Substring' means contiguous — we can't skip characters. The challenge is doing it in one pass instead of testing every substring for distinctness.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Substring or subsequence?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Substring — contiguous. We can't drop characters from the middle.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What characters can appear?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Any ASCII/Unicode: letters, digits, symbols, spaces. Don't assume lowercase-only.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I return the substring or its length?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just the length (an integer). The window's bounds give the substring if needed.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What about the empty string?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Length 0 — the loop never runs and best stays 0.

examples.explanation: The longest substring without repeats is "abc", length 3.
Only "b" has no repeat; the window can never exceed length 1.
"wke" (length 3). Note "pwke" is a subsequence, not a substring.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: A variable sliding window with a last-index map is the default; checking all substrings is the quadratic baseline.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Check Every Substring
approaches.whenToMention: Say it first to anchor the quadratic baseline and to motivate the sliding window.
hints: The answer is some substring. How would you test a single substring for 'all distinct'?
For each start index i, extend an end index j and keep a set of characters in [i..j]. Stop when you'd add a duplicate.
Track the longest clean window found over all starts. It re-scans overlapping ranges — that's the inefficiency to remove.
approaches.complexityReasoning: For each of n start indices, the inner extension does up to n work with O(1) set operations → O(n²) time. The set holds at most min(n, alphabet size) characters → O(min(n, Σ)) space.
approaches.explanation:
Fix a start index `i`. Extend an end index `j` rightward, adding each character to a set; the moment a character is already in the set, the substring `[i..j-1]` is the longest clean run starting at `i`. Record its length, then restart from `i+1`.

**Why this is the natural first attempt.** It directly encodes 'longest substring with all distinct characters' — try each start, grow until you can't. The set makes the distinctness test O(1) per step, so it's already better than re-checking each substring from scratch.

**Why we don't ship this.** Restarting the scan at every start index re-examines overlapping ranges over and over. With `n` up to `5 × 10⁴`, the quadratic blowup is too slow. The key waste: when we hit a duplicate starting at `i`, we throw away all the distinctness work and restart at `i+1`, even though most of that window is still valid. The sliding window keeps that work.
approaches.insight: When the inner loop hits a repeat, everything before the duplicate's first occurrence is still a valid window — restarting from i+1 discards that knowledge. A sliding window instead slides the left edge just past the conflict, reusing all the work in between.

dryRun.intro: For each start i, grow j with a set until a repeat appears.

code.python:
def lengthOfLongestSubstring(self, s: str) -> int:
    n = len(s)
    best = 0
    for i in range(n):
        seen = set()
        j = i
        while j < n and s[j] not in seen:
            seen.add(s[j])
            j += 1
        best = max(best, j - i)
    return best

pitfalls: Re-creating the set per start index — the source of the quadratic cost.
Off-by-one: the clean length is j - i, since j stopped on the duplicate.
Assuming a 26-letter alphabet when symbols and spaces are allowed.

approaches.name: Sliding Window + Last-Index Map (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'grow the window on the right; on a repeat, jump the left edge past the duplicate'.
hints: Instead of restarting at every start index, keep one window [left, right] that always holds distinct characters.
Store each character's last seen index. When the new character was seen at index p and p is inside the window (p >= left), the window must skip past p.
Jump left to p + 1 directly — no need to step it one at a time. Update the character's last index to right and track the max window length.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each index is visited once by `right`, and `left` only moves forward, so total pointer movement is O(n). The map holds at most one entry per distinct character → O(min(n, Σ)) space.
approaches.explanation:
Maintain a window `[left, right]` that is always free of repeats, plus a hash map `last` from character to the most recent index where it appeared. Slide `right` forward one character at a time.

**Handling a repeat with a jump, not a crawl.** When the character `c = s[right]` was last seen at index `p = last[c]`, and `p` is *inside* the current window (`p >= left`), then `c` would repeat. The fix is to move `left` to `p + 1` — instantly excluding the earlier `c` and everything before it. This is the whole speedup: instead of shrinking the window one step at a time, we leap the left edge directly past the conflict.

**Why the `p >= left` guard is essential.** The map remembers a character's last index *anywhere* in the string, even from before the current window. If that old index is to the left of `left`, the character is *not* in the window and there's no conflict — jumping to `p + 1` would move `left` *backward*, wrongly re-including characters and breaking the invariant. The guard ensures we only jump when the duplicate is genuinely inside the window, so `left` never regresses.

**Why update `last[c]` every iteration.** Whether or not we jumped, the current character's newest position is `right`, so we always set `last[c] = right`. Forgetting this when there's no jump would leave a stale index and corrupt future guards.

**Why one pass suffices.** `right` advances n times; `left` only ever moves forward and never passes `right`. Their combined movement is bounded by 2n, so the algorithm is linear — every character of work the brute force repeated is now done once.
approaches.insight: The map of last indices converts 'shrink the window until the duplicate is gone' into a single O(1) jump. The reusable lesson: when a window violation is caused by one known element, remembering where that element was lets you skip the left pointer straight past it instead of inching forward.

edgeCases.behavior: Empty string; loop never runs, best stays 0.

pitfalls: Omitting the `last[c] >= left` guard — left moves backward on duplicates outside the window (the classic 'abba' bug).
Not updating last[c] when there's no jump, leaving stale indices.
Computing the length as right − left (missing the +1).

commonMistakes: Moving the left pointer backward by jumping on a duplicate that's outside the current window.
Re-creating a set for every start index (the quadratic brute force).
Off-by-one in the window length (right − left vs right − left + 1).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the window guard (the 'abba' bug)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The map remembers a char's last index even outside the window. Without the >= left check, 'abba' jumps left backward to a stale position and overcounts.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting to update last[c] without a jump
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you only update last[c] when a jump happens, later guards read stale indices and the window logic breaks.

patternNote: Variable sliding window with a last-seen-index map. Reach for it on longest/shortest contiguous-window problems where a violation is caused by a single known element you can jump past. Same family as At Most K Distinct and Minimum Window Substring.
